I spent the last two weeks processing archival documents, and I thought it might be helpful to me to try and think out loud about what I'm doing. 

First of all, I'm noticing how wild it is that ordinary academics at mid-century had secretaries who typed their correspondence. The carbon copies on the onionskin paper with the initials of the secretaries below the signature; the "dictated but not signed" notice; the few handwritten notes when someone was writing from vacation are all remarkable windows into the lifeworld of the period. It's an occupation whose history I feel I should know more about. It makes me want to identify these people if possible through the books whose typing they surely did. Or perhaps the typists of books were different administrative support staff. 

The second thing I notice is how the densest correspondence is the most professional and business-like. The thickest folders are the ones with many letters produced by secretaries, meaning things the people whose archives I'm now sifting through did not feel it worth their time to write themselves. For letters they wrote themselves did not produce carbon copies. Or at least, I'm assuming this to be the case. In this way, the archive is rather less revealing than I want it to be. Or, rather, it is less *personally* revealing. It still reveals directions of thought, especially amid the ferment of an ongoing project. Letters show colleagues reaching out to one another to share ideas. But the letters typed by secretaries rarely give a glimpse behind the professional mask.

A better way to say it, however, is that what is revealed is always interpretive and inferential. In the two archives I have recently visited, folders tell a story that the principal wants posterity to hear. Thomas Szasz wants people like me to know that he was a friend to the civil rights movement in the early 1960s. Harold Lasswell wants people like me to know that he proposed forming an agency that would centralize intelligence functions at the same time that "Wild Bill" Donovan was. People want to be remembered in a certain way and for specific actions, arguments made, or positions taken relative to the history that they (at some point) realized they were living through. 

At first, this aspect of the archive was amusing to me: this desire to be seen a certain way. But in the end, I feel like it's a good impulse to consider how future generations will judge the documentary record. I think it's helpful to imagine that some unseen, and unthinkable, other will be sifting through your emails and drawing conclusions from them about the thoughts you had, and the kind of person you were. To want to be seen as virtuous seems to me a better way to be than to want to be seen as *not virtuous*. And to want to be remembered by future generations is to at least strive to do something worthy of remembrance. Who gets to be remembered has a lot to do with how we think about what "virtuous" means, so I realize these are not uncomplicated statements. But that has been the biggest shift in my thinking after spending time in two archives: to go from a kind of bemusement at the self-regard of these men to something less than admiration but more than indifference. For now, let's call it respect. I'm not sure that it will hold, but that's where I find myself at this moment.

The last thing I'll say is that I'm noticing how hard it is to make sense of anything. I have photographed so many letters and pieces of correspondence. Then, I write up my summary of what each letter says, trying to make sense of a conversation that I am usually tuning in to midstream. In most cases, I'm having to trust that something of use will emerge because its immediate relevance is not clear. In some cases, it's one or two sentences for every dozen letters. For others, it's one or two letters for every dozen folders. Either way, the hit rate is small. I'm finding that it's best not to think too hard about the low efficiency of the work and just be so thankful that I have the time and space to be doing it.
